# Finding and Fixing an Error

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-22, from the outline of the same day. Every number in the text is computed when the book builds. Needs dev dplR 1.8.1 for the ring-edit methods and `xdate.report`. Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

## Big Idea

[Crossdating a Collection](05Crossdating.qmd) ended with two flagged series in Mesa Verde, each error placed within a 50-year segment. This chapter takes an error from a segment to a year, puts the ring back, and checks the result. The order of work doesn't change from one collection to the next. Narrow the window with the statistics, look at the core, make the edit, run the report again. The statistics never make the edit on their own. Pilcher put it plainly in the methods book most of us call the Cook Book: a computer makes crossdating faster and easier, and it doesn't make it any better [@Pilcher1990].

A word about expectations first. Mesa Verde is about as good as correlations get in dendrochronology. Everything in the last chapter worked cleanly because those trees agree so well, and if that's all you see you'll expect too much of your own collection. So Mesa Verde gets one short section here. Most of the chapter is about Hurricane Ridge, an ordinary collection that as far as anyone knows is dated correctly, and about the simulated stand, where we know the answer. The second half is about flags nobody planted, because in most collections most flags are not dating errors, and telling which ones are is the skill.

## Packages

```{r}
#| label: fix-setup
#| message: false
library(dplR)
source("R/plant-dating-errors.R")
source("R/sim-collection.R")
co021 <- read.rwl("data/co021.rwl", format = "tucson")
wa082 <- read.rwl("data/wa082.rwl", format = "tucson")
co021Bad <- plant.dating.errors()
wa082Bad <- plant.wa082.error()
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-words
#| include: false
# spell out zero through nine in the prose
words <- function(n, cap = FALSE) {
  out <- as.character(n)
  small <- n %in% 0:9
  out[small] <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six",
                  "seven", "eight", "nine")[n[small] + 1]
  if (cap) substr(out, 1, 1) <- toupper(substr(out, 1, 1))
  out
}
```

`co021Bad` is Mesa Verde with the two errors from the last chapter. `wa082Bad` is Hurricane Ridge with one: series 712031 has lost its 1850 ring.

## The Clean Case, Briefly

`corr.series.seg` takes one series and correlates its segments with a master built from the others, and adds a running correlation underneath.

```{r}
#| label: fix-css-645221
#| fig-cap: "Series 645221 in Mesa Verde, with its 1797 ring deleted. Horizontal bars are 50-year segments, the curve is a running correlation, and the dashed line is the critical value."
css645 <- corr.series.seg(co021Bad, series = "645221", seg.length = 50)
```

That's the report's row for 645221 drawn at a finer grain. The correlation sits near zero until the late 1700s and then climbs to where the rest of the collection lives. Somewhere in the climb is the missing ring.

`ccf.series.rwl` goes the rest of the way. It cuts the series into short segments, here 20 years overlapping by 10, and correlates each with the master at a range of lags. Cut the collection down to the years around the problem with `window` first. What comes back is a table of correlations, one column for each 20-year segment and one row for each lag, here 11 rows by 14 columns. Rather than read all of them, a three-line helper, `bestLag`, picks out the lag with the highest correlation in each column. The rest of the chapter uses it too.

```{r}
#| label: fix-ccf-645221
ccf645 <- ccf.series.rwl(window(co021Bad, 1700, 1850), series = "645221",
                         seg.length = 20, bin.floor = 0, make.plot = FALSE)

# ccf645$ccf is a table with one column per 20-year bin and one row per lag,
# named "lag.-5" to "lag.5". For each column, find the row with the highest
# correlation and turn its name into a number.
bestLag <- function(ccfResult) {
  lags <- as.numeric(sub("lag.", "", rownames(ccfResult$ccf)))
  apply(ccfResult$ccf, 2, function(column) lags[which.max(column)])
}
bestLag(ccf645)
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-ccf-co021-numbers
#| include: false
ccf643 <- ccf.series.rwl(window(co021Bad, 1350, 1500), series = "643143",
                         seg.length = 20, bin.floor = 0, make.plot = FALSE)
lag645 <- bestLag(ccf645)
lag643 <- bestLag(ccf643)
binStart <- function(b) as.numeric(sub("\\..*", "", b))
binRange <- function(b) sub("\\.", " to ", b)
lastBin <- function(l, lag) names(l)[max(which(l == lag))]
firstBin <- function(l, lag) names(l)[min(which(l == lag))]
r645 <- ccf645$ccf
```

Every bin through `r binRange(lastBin(lag645, -1))` lines up best at lag -1, with correlations around `r sprintf("%.2f", median(r645["lag.-1", lag645 == -1]))`, and every bin from `r binRange(firstBin(lag645, 0))` onward lines up at lag 0, around `r sprintf("%.2f", median(r645["lag.0", lag645 == 0]))`. The years those two bins share, the 1790s, are where the ring went missing, and the ring I deleted was 1797. The same treatment of 643143, the false ring, has its last bin at lag +1 in `r binRange(lastBin(lag643, 1))` and its first at lag 0 in `r binRange(firstBin(lag643, 0))`, which puts the error in the 1420s. The planted year is 1425. A negative lag is a missing ring and a positive one is a false ring, as in the last chapter.

Correlations near 0.9 in 20-year bins are what Mesa Verde gives you. Now look at an ordinary collection.

## An Ordinary Collection

```{r}
#| label: fix-report-wa082
wa082Report <- xdate.report(wa082Bad)
wa082Flags <- wa082Report$flagged
wa082Flags[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag", "weak")]
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-report-wa082-numbers
#| include: false
f031 <- wa082Flags[wa082Flags$series == "712031", ]
fOther <- wa082Flags[wa082Flags$series != "712031", ]
```

The planted error is there: 712031 is flagged B at lag -1 in `r words(nrow(f031[f031$flag == "B", ]))` segments, with correlations of `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", f031$r.lag[f031$flag == "B"]), collapse = " and ")` at the lag, and then A in `r f031$from[f031$flag == "A"]` to `r f031$to[f031$flag == "A"]`. That A is the segment that straddles the error, half misdated and half not, so it fits badly where it is and no better anywhere else. It's the commonest way a real error shows up at the end of its run of B flags. And it isn't alone. `r words(nrow(fOther), cap = TRUE)` other segments are flagged in series that nobody touched, which is how a real error usually looks: one problem among several things that look like problems.

Here is `ccf.series.rwl` on 712031, drawn this time.

```{r}
#| label: fix-ccf-712031
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Cross-correlations of 712031 with the master in 20-year bins overlapping by 10, from 1790 to 1910. Read the panels from the bottom left, along each row and then up. Dashed lines are the critical value."
ccf031 <- ccf.series.rwl(window(wa082Bad, 1790, 1910), series = "712031",
                         seg.length = 20, bin.floor = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-ccf-712031-numbers
#| include: false
lag031 <- bestLag(ccf031)
r031 <- ccf031$ccf
muddled <- names(lag031)[lag031 == -2]
ccf031b <- ccf.series.rwl(window(wa082Bad, 1790, 1910), series = "712031",
                          seg.length = 30, bin.floor = 0, make.plot = FALSE)
lag031b <- bestLag(ccf031b)
```

It works, but look at the difference from Mesa Verde. At lag -1 the early bins correlate between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(r031["lag.-1", lag031 == -1]))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(r031["lag.-1", lag031 == -1]))`. One bin, `r binRange(muddled)`, points nowhere useful: its best lag is -2, at only `r sprintf("%.2f", r031["lag.-2", muddled])`, which is no dating error anyone planted. It's what a bin straddling an error looks like when the signal is ordinary. From the `r binRange(firstBin(lag031, 0))` bin on, lag 0 wins at `r sprintf("%.2f", min(r031["lag.0", lag031 == 0]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(r031["lag.0", lag031 == 0]))`. The last bin at lag -1 is `r binRange(lastBin(lag031, -1))` and the first at lag 0 is `r binRange(firstBin(lag031, 0))`, with the muddled bin between them, so the error is somewhere from the 1840s to the early 1850s. The planted year is 1850. Short segments trade reliability for resolution, and at Hurricane Ridge 20 years is near the edge. With 30-year bins the last bin at lag -1 is `r binRange(lastBin(lag031b, -1))` and the first at lag 0 is `r binRange(firstBin(lag031b, 0))`. No bin points anywhere else, and the years the two share hold the error.

The last statistical step is the one Douglass would recognize. `xskel.ccf.plot` draws a skeleton plot of the series above one of the master for a window of years, with the cross-correlations for each half underneath.

```{r}
#| label: fix-xskel-712031
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Skeleton plots of 712031 (top) and the master (bottom) for 1830 to 1870, with cross-correlations for each 20-year half. Long bars are narrow rings."
xskel.ccf.plot(wa082Bad, series = "712031", win.start = 1830, win.width = 40)
```

Look at the marker years, the narrow rings that get long bars. Before 1850 the series' markers fall one year after the master's: 1836 against 1835, 1841 against 1840. After it, 1852, 1864 and 1866 line up in both. Something happened in 712031 around 1850, and the master has a narrow ring in 1850, which is exactly the kind of year a ring goes missing in.

That is as far as the statistics go. The next step is the core. On a mounted, sanded core you'd look at the rings around 1850 under the microscope for a ring that pinches out or a micro ring squeezed against its neighbor. The other core from the same tree is the first thing to check against, since it should share the tree's missing rings and its own dating stands or falls separately. For a false ring you'd look for a density change inside a ring that doesn't end in a sharp boundary. Pilcher's account of crossdating is good on all of this, and on the error that has nothing to do with the tree: a decade miscounted when the measurements were written down, which is what the dots every ten years on a mounted core are for [@Pilcher1990, p. 45].

## Putting the Rings Back

`insert.ring` and `delete.ring` take the collection, the series and the year.

```{r}
#| label: fix-edits
co021Fixed <- insert.ring(co021Bad, series = "645221", year = 1797, ring.value = 0)
co021Fixed <- delete.ring(co021Fixed, series = "643143", year = 1425)
wa082Fixed <- insert.ring(wa082Bad, series = "712031", year = 1850, ring.value = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-edits-check
#| include: false
same <- function(a, b, s) {
  ya <- time(a)[!is.na(a[[s]])]
  yb <- time(b)[!is.na(b[[s]])]
  identical(ya, yb)
}
dates645 <- same(co021, co021Fixed, "645221")
dates031 <- same(wa082, wa082Fixed, "712031")
width1797 <- co021[["645221"]][time(co021) == 1797]
values643 <- isTRUE(all.equal(co021[["643143"]], co021Fixed[["643143"]][match(time(co021), time(co021Fixed))]))
alt643 <- delete.ring(co021Bad, series = "643143", year = 1424)
values643alt <- isTRUE(all.equal(co021[["643143"]], alt643[["643143"]][match(time(co021), time(alt643))]))
stopifnot(dates645, dates031, values643, values643alt)
```

Inserting a ring of zero width says the ring is locally absent on this radius, which is what a missing ring found on the core usually is. The dates come back exactly: 645221 and 712031 run over the same years they did before I broke them. The width doesn't. The ring I deleted from 645221 was `r width1797` mm wide, and nothing in the statistics could have told you that. They find where a ring is missing and say nothing about how wide it was. Only the sample, or another radius from the same tree, can say.

Deleting the 1425 ring puts 643143 back exactly. So would deleting 1424, because the false ring I planted is a copy of its neighbor. Which of two rings is the false one is a question for the core under a microscope.

Both functions hold the outer year fixed and move the rings inside it, which is what you want for a core from a living tree, where the outer ring is the year you cored it. A floating series has no year to hold, and [Dating a Floater](07Floaters.qmd) deals with that.

Now check the work.

```{r}
#| label: fix-recheck
nrow(xdate.report(co021Fixed)$flagged)
wa082FixedFlags <- xdate.report(wa082Fixed)$flagged
unique(wa082FixedFlags$series)
```

Mesa Verde has no flags. Hurricane Ridge is back to its own `r words(nrow(wa082FixedFlags))`, none of them in 712031. And keep the script. Those three lines are the record of what you changed and why, attached to the original file. xDateR writes the same kind of record for you when you edit there.

## Flags Nobody Planted

So what about Hurricane Ridge's other flags? Before deciding, practice on a collection where the answer is known. The simulated stand from [Chapter 2](02CoresToRecord.qmd) has one dating error, a missing ring in SIM03A at 1800, and nothing else.

```{r}
#| label: fix-sim
sim <- sim.collection(seed = 1)
simFlags <- xdate.report(sim$rwl)$flagged
simFlags[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag", "gain", "weak")]
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-sim-numbers
#| include: false
s03 <- simFlags[simFlags$series == "SIM03A", ]
s03run <- s03[s03$best.lag == -1, ]                 # the run before the error
s03mid <- s03[s03$from < 1800 & s03$to > 1800, ]    # the segment across it
s10 <- simFlags[simFlags$series == "SIM10A", ]
crit <- qt(0.99, 48) / sqrt(48 + qt(0.99, 48)^2)    # 50-year segments
```

SIM03A looks like 712031: B flags at lag -1 with gains of `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", s03run$gain), collapse = " and ")` in the segments before the error. The segment that straddles it, `r s03mid$from`-`r s03mid$to`, is flagged too, at lag `r sprintf("%+d", s03mid$best.lag)` with a gain of only `r sprintf("%.2f", s03mid$gain)`, and it is marked weak. In 712031 the same segment got an A. Either way the report is saying the same thing: half of the segment is dated right and half is a year off, so no single shift fits it.

SIM10A is the one that is dated correctly, and I know because I built it. Its segment from `r s10$from` to `r s10$to` correlates with the master at `r sprintf("%.3f", s10$r.dated)` where it is dated, a little under the critical value of `r sprintf("%.3f", crit)`, and shifted `r abs(s10$best.lag)` years it correlates at `r sprintf("%.3f", s10$r.lag)`, `r if (abs(s10$r.lag - crit) < 0.005) "right at it" else if (s10$r.lag > crit) "a little above it" else "still under it"`. The gain is `r sprintf("%.3f", s10$gain)`. For that shift to be real, the core would need `r words(abs(s10$best.lag))` rings missing inside one 50-year segment and none anywhere else. A segment that fits poorly where it is, and only slightly better at a shift no core could plausibly need, is noise.

Now Hurricane Ridge as it comes.

```{r}
#| label: fix-wa082-as-is
wa082Flags0 <- xdate.report(wa082)$flagged
wa082Flags0[, c("series", "from", "to", "flag", "r.dated", "best.lag", "r.lag", "weak")]
```

```{r}
#| label: fix-wa082-as-is-numbers
#| include: false
b0 <- wa082Flags0[wa082Flags0$flag == "B", ]
a0 <- wa082Flags0[wa082Flags0$flag == "A", ]
crit <- qt(0.99, 48) / sqrt(48 + qt(0.99, 48)^2)
```

The `r words(nrow(b0))` B flags are all marked weak, at lags of `r paste(sprintf("%+d", b0$best.lag), collapse = ", ")`. A misdated core can be off by more than a ring, but a shift of eight or nine years in a segment that fits no better there than anywhere else looks like SIM10A again: a big shift for a small gain. The `r words(nrow(a0))` A flags, in `r paste(a0$series, collapse = " and ")`, correlate at `r paste(sprintf("%.3f", a0$r.dated), collapse = " and ")` against a critical value of `r sprintf("%.3f", crit)`. That is low agreement just under a line, in a collection whose segments are often not far above it, and both are best where they're dated. As far as anyone knows, Hurricane Ridge is dated correctly, and nothing here argues otherwise.

What, then, makes a B flag worth pulling a core out of the drawer for? A gain of a few tenths. A lag of one or two years. A run of segments that agree on the lag, and a clean switch back to lag 0 where the run ends, often with an A flag on the segment in between. 712031's planted ring has all of that. None of the flags nobody planted has any of it. In a collection as strong as Mesa Verde even a lone B flag deserves a look, and in an ordinary one I'd wait for the pattern before pulling anything.

## Wrapping Up

The statistics placed every planted error to within a decade or so, the skeleton plot showed the shift in the marker years, and `insert.ring` and `delete.ring` put the rings back with the outer year held fixed. The statistics couldn't say how wide a missing ring was or which of two rings was the false one, and on Hurricane Ridge they flagged `r words(nrow(wa082Flags0))` segments in a collection with no known errors. Those are questions for the sample.

The next chapter, [Dating a Floater](07Floaters.qmd), is about a series with no outer year to hold fixed.

## Exercises

1. Narrow 712031 with 10-year segments. Where does it stop being reliable? Do the same for 645221 at Mesa Verde and compare.
2. Insert the missing ring in 645221 with `ring.value = mean(co021Bad[["645221"]], na.rm = TRUE)` instead of zero, detrend, and compare `rwi.stats` with the zero version. Does the choice of width matter for anything downstream?
3. Look at SIM10A's flagged segment with `ccf.series.rwl` and `xskel.ccf.plot`. Would you have pulled the core?
4. Pick one of Hurricane Ridge's A flags and decide what you'd do about it. Does the other core from the same tree help?
5. Plant a missing ring in a weak simulated stand, `sim.collection(rbar.bt = 0.2, rbar.wt = 0.4, seed = 1)`, and try to find it with this chapter's tools.

## Further Reading

- @Pilcher1990 is the chapter on sample preparation, crossdating and measurement in *Methods of Dendrochronology*. It is short and practical: how to prepare a core, how to crossdate it, the decade error, and why you shouldn't expect to crossdate a sequence much shorter than about 40 years.
- @GrissinoMayer2001 walks through what to do with each part of COFECHA's output, including the flagged segments.
- @Black2016 shows what errors that slip through do to a chronology downstream.
